rationale.id_bands: Numbers 1-20 are in use and 21-49 are reserved by futureBuckets for the chronological backfill (Late Antiquity -> Pre-LLM AI). Non-linear eras therefore get dedicated bands so the chronological space stays clean: 100-119 thematic, 120-139 crisis, 140-159 regional. 25 (Islamic Golden Age) and 50 (AI Inflection Point) are legacy entries in the chronological space and stay put.
rationale.kind: chronological = the linear sweep the corpus was built on; thematic = a Big-History lens crossing geography; crisis = an episode of rupture, suffering or environmental shock; regional = a civilisational sphere outside the Western default.
rationale.tone: Drives palette. golden = flourishing; sombre = atrocity/rupture, muted palette, no celebratory framing; neutral = everything else. This is data, not a CSS special-case, so the UI never hardcodes a list of 'sad eras'.
rationale.care_level: high = the era covers mass atrocity, enslavement or genocide. Editorial duty of care applies: sourcing triangulated beyond the corpus, naming conventions checked, no single-source claims about victim counts. Per operator decision 2026-07-29 this is NOT a hard publish gate, but it IS a research-depth and provenance-display requirement.
rationale.overlaps: All non-chronological eras overlap each other and the chronological sweep by design. The index builder must not assume disjointness.

thematic.label: The Scientific Revolution
thematic.focus: The shift from natural philosophy to modern science: Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, Newton, the experimental method and the founding of the learned societies.

thematic.label: The Age of Revolutions
thematic.focus: American, French, Haitian and the 1848 European revolutions; absolutist monarchy giving way to representative government. The Haitian Revolution is the canonical multi-era event: this, Abolition, and the chronological Modern sweep.

thematic.label: The Industrial Age
thematic.focus: Mechanised manufacturing, urbanisation, the factory system, and the social dislocation that followed.

thematic.label: The Era of Decolonisation
thematic.focus: The dismantling of European colonial empires across Asia and Africa after WWII, including the partitions and wars that accompanied it.

thematic.label: The Digital & Information Age
thematic.focus: Computing, networking and the internet reorganising economy and society. Abuts era-50 (AI Inflection Point) deliberately; they overlap rather than succeed one another.

thematic.label: The Age of Abolition & Emancipation
thematic.focus: From the early British and French abolitionist societies to the Lei Aurea in Brazil (1888). Paired with era-120; neither should be read without the other.

crisis.label: The Transatlantic Slave Trade
crisis.focus: The forced migration of an estimated 10-12 million enslaved Africans to the Americas. Must cross-reference European and American economic expansion against African demographic and political devastation in the same years — the two are one event seen from two ends.
crisis.careNotes: Figures are contested and vary by database (Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database vs older estimates). Show the range and its provenance, never a single confident number.

crisis.label: The Era of Modern Genocide & Mass Atrocity
crisis.focus: From the Herero and Namaqua genocide (1904) through the Holodomor, the Holocaust, Cambodia, Rwanda, Srebrenica and after. A lens on the extremes of state power and ethnic violence.
crisis.careNotes: Naming conventions are themselves contested and politically live. Attribute every designation to its source. Victim counts must never rest on a single source. No aggregate 'ranking' of atrocities.

crisis.label: The Age of the World Wars
crisis.focus: WWI, the interwar period and WWII as one continuous era, letting the user filter the densest 31 years in the corpus.

crisis.label: The Black Death & Crisis of the Late Middle Ages
crisis.focus: The most fatal recorded pandemic and the demographic, economic and religious restructuring that followed — including the pogroms it triggered.
crisis.careNotes: Mortality estimates (commonly 'up to half of Europe') are actively revised by paleogenomics and regional studies. Present as a contested range.

crisis.label: The Late Antique Little Ice Age & Justinianic Plague
crisis.focus: Volcanic dust-veil cooling from 536 CE, crop failure, and the first bubonic plague pandemic destabilising the Byzantine and Sasanian empires.
crisis.careNotes: The maximalist reading (climate + plague caused imperial collapse) is contested by revisionist work arguing far smaller demographic effects. Both positions must appear.

crisis.label: The Little Ice Age
crisis.focus: Centuries of regional cooling reshaping agriculture, migration and conflict, chiefly in the Northern Hemisphere. Deliberately overlaps eras 100-102 and 123.
crisis.careNotes: Neither globally synchronous nor uniform. Avoid framing it as a single worldwide event; the brainstorm's cited source for this item is not scholarly and must be replaced.

crisis.label: The Cold War & Proxy Conflicts
crisis.focus: Bipolar confrontation, the nuclear arms race, espionage, and the proxy wars that carried most of the actual casualties. Overlaps Decolonisation (era-103) heavily and intentionally.

crisis.label: The Era of Atlantic Piracy & Privateering
crisis.focus: Maritime conflict, state-licensed privateering and economic disruption in the Atlantic and Caribbean — the same sea lanes and the same decades as era-120, which is the point of running them in parallel.

regional.label: The West African Golden Age
regional.focus: The overlapping heights of the Mali and Songhai empires: trans-Saharan trade, Timbuktu and the Sankore scholarly tradition, and state formation.
regional.careNotes: The record leans heavily on Arabic-language external observers (Ibn Battuta, al-Umari) plus oral tradition (the Sunjata epic). Source provenance must be visible, not flattened into neutral narration.

regional.label: The Rise of the Caliphates
regional.focus: Political and military expansion of the Rashidun, Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates. Deliberately overlaps era-25 (Islamic Golden Age), which covers the intellectual flowering; this covers the polity.

regional.label: The Tang & Song Cosmopolitan Era
regional.focus: Cultural flowering and the Song commercial revolution: woodblock and movable-type printing, the compass, gunpowder, paper money, and the examination system.

regional.label: The Mongol Peace (Pax Mongolica)
regional.focus: Mongol conquest enabling unprecedented cross-continental trade and exchange along the Silk Road — and the plague that travelled the same routes into era-123.
regional.careNotes: 'Peace' is the historiographic label for the trade regime, not a description of the conquests that produced it. The framing must carry that tension rather than resolve it.

regional.label: The Edo Period
regional.focus: Tokugawa Japan: internal peace, urbanisation, a flourishing merchant culture, and the sakoku restrictions on foreign contact.
regional.careNotes: 'Closed country' is an overstatement long since revised — trade continued via Nagasaki, Tsushima, Satsuma and Matsumae.

regional.label: The Classic Maya Period
regional.focus: Peak Maya urbanisation, monumental architecture, the Long Count calendar and astronomy, and the political fragmentation at the era's close.
regional.careNotes: 'Collapse' is contested — it describes the end of a dynastic and monumental order, not of Maya people or culture, who are continuous to the present. Wording matters here.

regional.label: The Imperial Andes
regional.focus: The rapid expansion and administrative complexity of Tawantinsuyu (the Inca empire) — khipu record-keeping, the road system, mit'a labour — up to the Spanish conquest.
regional.careNotes: Nearly all textual sources are post-conquest Spanish or mestizo chronicles. Provenance must be shown; khipu remain only partially deciphered.
